Can AI in energy systems become a development opportunity, or will it deepen existing divides?

AI-enabled forecasting and optimization could unlock up to 175 GW of additional transmission capacity from existing power lines, without building a single new one. Improved forecasting has already increased wind power market value by up to 20% in some systems, while AI-driven fault detection can reduce outage durations by 30 to 50%.

But the stakes are equally high. Some of the largest AI data centres now consume as much electricity as around 2 million households, while more than 2,500 GW of renewable, storage, and large-load projects remain stuck in grid queues globally. The story can go one of two ways. If we are not careful, AI can push energy systems beyond what people and the planet can sustain. If we are deliberate, it can strengthen resilience and fairness.

This is what I will be exploring today at the University of Cambridge in a lecture titled "What Will Your Knowledge Make Possible?" with the next generation of energy leaders, looking at how energy, digital systems, and AI are converging into what I call planetary intelligence, and three priorities that stand out:

🔹 Treat energy data as public infrastructure to unlock investment at scale. Shared intelligence on demand, grid capacity, and system performance can reduce uncertainty and accelerate investment.
🔹 Govern AI and energy within land, water, and social limits. AI infrastructure cannot be planned outside ecological realities and resource constraints.
🔹 Measure success by access, resilience, and opportunity for people. The value of energy intelligence is ultimately measured through jobs, services, and human outcomes.

The future of energy is not something we simply predict. It is something we collectively build. Looking forward to today's conversation in #Cambridge University and to hearing perspectives from the next generation helping shape what comes next.
